body_markdown:
Before we discuss Tony Bevacqua’s love of the Chevrolet Corvette, it may be helpful to learn a bit about his background.


He had a long, distinguished career as a U.S. Air Force military pilot, with a pair of assignments that other pilots (and plenty of others) only dream about: Flying the U-2 “Dragon Lady” spy plane at altitudes of 70,000 feet or higher, followed by seven years at the helm of its spiritual successor, the (comparatively) fire-breathing SR-71 “Blackbird,” capable of flying at 85,000 feet. He became one of only 40 pilots who saw service in both the U-2 and the SR-71.


USAF/Luis Ruiz-Vazquez


What did he do after he retired? Perhaps do what many former military pilots did, move to the airlines to fly passengers? “Not me,” said retired Lt. Col. Tony Bevacqua. “I was never interested in that. I did all the flying I wanted in the military.”


In fact, he gave up flying altogether. Before he enlisted at age 18, he had never been near an airplane. He told the recruiters that he wanted to be a pilot, only because “that was the best thing you could be in the Air Force, right? Basically, I enlisted because I was looking for a job. And that’s the job they gave me.”


In 1952, fresh out of high school, one of several “strange occurrences,” as he calls them, took place: As he stood in the military recruitment line, he learned that the Air Force had just dropped the requirement that an airman must have a college education. “You could even become a pilot with just a high school education,” Bevacqua recalled. Sounds good, he thought; sign me up.


USAF


USAF


After basic training, he began pilot training in 1953 and graduated in 1954. He was sent to Georgia to fly the 600-mph F-84 Thunderjet fighter.


Soon, though, he was plucked from the ranks and told to move to Groom Lake in Nevada, which may have been a lake eons ago, but was now a dry lakebed certifiably in the middle of nowhere. Perhaps you know Groom Lake by the name it acquired later: Area 51.


It was a perfect place to learn to fly the top-secret U-2, an airplane Bevacqua knew nothing about. “We’d never heard of it,” he said. “It was secret, and it was classified.” But he soon learned everything he needed to know about the slow, spindly airplane, essentially a glider with an engine. It was designed to take off, then slowly climb to its designated altitude of about 70,000 feet. No enemy planes could go that high, and no weapons could hit a U-2. You flew by yourself, wearing what he calls the “monkey suit,” a very heavy space suit that piped in pure oxygen. “It was lonely,” Bevacqua said. “And boring.” Missions could be 10 hours long.


The boring aspect may have changed in 1960, when Francis Gary Powers was shot down over Russia. He somehow survived and was captured. Powers and Bevacqua had been roommates until Powers literally disappeared one night, spirited away to fly the U-2 for the CIA.


John Bryson/Getty Images


U-2 pilots had been given a dose of deadly poison hidden inside a silver dollar, which they wore around their neck to take if it was inevitable that they would be captured by enemy forces. Powers declined to use it. Many in the U.S. branded him a traitor, others as a hero. After years of grandstanding and celebrations by Russian leader Nikita Khrushchev, the imprisoned Powers was sent home, swapped for a Russian prisoner that the U.S. held. Powers finished out his aviation career flying a traffic helicopter in California, in which he crashed and died.


Tony Bevacqua continued to fly U-2 missions for the Air Force, mostly photographing what was beneath him, and sampling any nuclear radiation he came across. Then he quit flying to attend the Air Force Command and Staff College in Alabama. As soon as he graduated, he was asked if he’d be interested in[flying the SR-71](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/buick-nailheads-were-the-engines-behind-the-engines-in-the-sr-71-blackbird/) , the 2200-mph reconnaissance jet that once flew between New York to London in one hour and 54 minutes, a record.


U.S. National Archives


Yes, he would, he said. “Now that was an airplane!” he recalled. Bevacqua was based at Beale Air Force Base in Northern California. He never left. He retired in March of 1973 as a lieutenant colonel, with 738 hours in the SR-71, settling in the Yuba City area, working in real estate and as an advocate for saving Beale Air Force base, from which modified U-2 spy planes, which were first flown in 1955, still operate.


And now (finally!) we get to what Colonel Bevacqua did in his retirement: Trading in Corvettes. “Collect them?” he said: “I’m not so sure I was collecting them. I was buying them and selling them all the time. I don’t think I ever had more than four at once.”


Mecum


Mecum


Mecum


Mecum


Mecum


The Corvette was a car Bevacqua said he has “liked for a hundred years!” Well, close; he’s now 92, and said his memory isn’t what it was when he was just, say, 90. He didn’t have a favorite—“I like them all,” he recalled—but it appears he was partial to one Corvette that sold at the Mecum Auction’s debut event in Nashville last week.


Mecum


It was one of those Corvettes he bought, then sold, and the current owner considered the Arctic White, 755-horsepower 2019 Corvette ZR1 a tribute to Bevacqua, who personally signed the console lid. Its Michigan license plate reads: “U2 SR71.” The 5479-mile example sold for $155,100.


Behind the wheel of one of his Corvettes, Bevacqua said he satisfied his need for speed “by watching the telephone poles fly by faster and faster.” For the U-2 and SR-71 pilot, that was enough.
